ig_caption:
On an F-1 visa since 2021 or earlier? 2026 may be the year your tax status changes.

✔️ For your first 5 calendar years, F-1 students usually don't count their days toward the IRS 183-day test, so most stay nonresidents.
✔️ Any part of a year counts as one of the 5. Arrived in December 2021? That was year one.
✔️ In year 6, your days count. Pass the 183-day test and you're usually a resident for tax (narrow exceptions apply).
✔️ Residents file Form 1040, and Social Security and Medicare apply to OPT pay. Nonresidents file Form 8843, plus Form 1040-NR if they had US income.

Filed the wrong form for an earlier year? An amended return can fix it.

Comment F1 and we'll send you the link, or find it at mfa-advisory.com/international-students

General information, not tax advice.

li_caption:
Many international students assume they stay nonresidents for tax as long as they hold an F-1 visa. The IRS rule runs on calendar years, and year 6 is where it often changes.

1. F-1 students are usually exempt individuals for their first 5 calendar years, so their days don't count toward the 183-day substantial presence test.
2. Any part of a calendar year counts as one of the 5. A student who arrived in December 2021 used 2021 as year one.
3. From year 6, the days count. Meeting the 183-day test usually makes the student a resident alien for tax, unless they establish they don't intend to live in the US permanently and have complied with their visa.
4. Resident aliens file Form 1040 and report worldwide income, and the F-1 exemption from Social Security and Medicare tax no longer applies to their wages, including OPT pay.
5. Nonresidents file Form 8843, plus Form 1040-NR if they have US income to report.

If the wrong return went in for an earlier year, an amended return can fix it. We check residency and prepare the right forms.

Comment F1 and we will send it.

Link in the first comment.
